video_caption: In a lab setting, a person wearing blue gloves is shown holding a small test tube filled with red liquid, likely blood, in their left hand. The test tube has a purple stopper and a white label with "386" printed on it. Arranged neatly on a white, textured surface are six clear, rectangular glass slides, each with a frosted end, laid out in two parallel rows. The person uses their right hand to gently touch and arrange the slides before removing the purple stopper from the blood-filled test tube.

A person wearing blue medical gloves and a blue lab coat holds a white box of "Fisherbrand Frosted Beveled Edge Microscope Slides Precleaned". The label also displays "Ordering Information: Catalog No. 12-549-6, Size: 3" x 1" x 1.0mm, Quantity: Approx. 72 Gross, Made in Hungary of Swiss Glass", along with the Fisher Scientific logo. The scene then shifts to a white textured surface where several clear microscope slides are laid out. The person, still in blue gloves, demonstrates the correct technique for placing blood drops on slides using a red-filled capillary tube. First, they show an inadequately filled capillary tube, resulting in a very tiny blood drop on a slide, which in turn creates a small, poor-quality blood smear. Next, they demonstrate taking an excessive amount of blood from the tube, leading to a very large, unwieldy blood drop on another slide, also deemed unsuitable for a good smear. Finally, they illustrate the correct method: filling a capillary tube about three-quarters full by holding it at an angle, then depositing a medium-sized, perfectly rounded drop of blood onto a slide, positioned just above the frosted edge, which is stated as the ideal amount for making quality blood smears.

A pair of hands, encased in blue gloves, is positioned over a white, textured surface. Three rectangular glass slides are laid horizontally on the surface, each featuring a small, circular drop of red liquid towards one end. In the bottom right corner, one of the gloved hands holds a small, clear tube filled with red liquid, while the other gloved hand carefully places another empty glass slide near the lower rightmost slide that already has a red drop.

In this video segment, a person wearing blue gloves demonstrates incorrect methods for preparing blood smears on glass microscope slides. The scene is set on a white, textured surface. Initially, a small drop of red liquid, presumably blood, is placed on a clear glass slide using a thin red rod. The gloved hand then takes a second slide, positions it behind the blood drop, and pulls it forward, resulting in a thick, uneven blood smear. The demonstrator explains this is incorrect as it creates an undesirable shape and lacks control. Next, a fresh drop of blood is placed on another clean slide. The gloved hand uses a spreader slide, placing it on the blood drop and pushing it forward with too much pressure, which is audibly described as "grinding." This also leads to a thick and uneven smear. Finally, on a third slide with a new blood drop, the spreader slide is held too high, causing a "shaky slide syndrome" and resulting in a wobbly, inconsistent smear as the blood is spread. The segment concludes with the demonstrator stating they will show the correct method, but the video ends before this is shown.

A person wearing blue gloves and a light blue lab coat sleeve is preparing blood smears on glass slides. Initially, three clear rectangular glass slides are laid out horizontally on a white, textured surface. The gloved hand uses a thin, clear stick to carefully place a small, circular red blood drop onto one end of each of the three slides. Then, the person picks up a fourth clear slide, which serves as a spreader. Holding the spreader at an angle (around 45 degrees, as mentioned by the speaker), the gloved hand brings it into contact with the first blood drop on the rightmost slide. Once the blood evenly spreads across the edge of the spreader slide, the person quickly and smoothly draws the spreader across the entire length of the slide, creating a thin, elongated reddish smear. This process is then repeated for the second and third slides, resulting in three completed blood smears. The person briefly picks up one of the smeared slides to show the finished product.

In this brief segment, the camera is focused on a cluster of rectangular glass slides, laid out on a white, textured surface, likely a lab bench covered with a disposable mat. Each slide features a small, reddish-brown smudge, consistent with dried blood smears. Three slides are clearly visible in the foreground, with their smudges distinct, while a few more are blurred in the background. The lighting is bright and even, highlighting the clear glass and the reddish samples.

The video segment opens at 0:05 with a gloved hand holding a microscope slide that has a red smear on its clear portion and a frosted end. Another gloved hand uses a black marker to write on the frosted end of the slide, then moves the marker away, followed by the first hand slightly adjusting the slide's position on a white, textured surface. At 0:31, the scene cuts to show four small, clear glass containers with lids, lined up on the same white surface. Each container holds a different colored liquid: teal, red, dark blue/black (with a small blue dot on its surface), and clear. The text "PROTOCOL Hema 3 Stain" appears in white on a black background in the upper right corner, identifying the staining method being prepared.

The video segment shows four small, clear glass containers lined up on a white paper towel. Each container holds a different colored liquid: turquoise (leftmost), red, dark blue/black, and clear (rightmost). Clear plastic lids are placed next to the two rightmost containers. Text in the upper right corner reads "PROTOCOL Hema 3 Stain." At the 00:07 mark, a hand wearing a blue glove enters the frame from the left, holding a clear glass slide with a faint red smear on it. The hand moves the slide slowly towards the leftmost container, which contains the turquoise liquid, seemingly preparing to dip it.

A person wearing a light blue lab coat and blue latex gloves is seen in a lab-like setting, performing an experiment with four clear glass beakers arranged in a row on a white surface. From left to right, the beakers contain a light blue/teal liquid, a red liquid, a dark blue/black liquid, and a clear liquid. The person uses a long, thin, flexible white tool, possibly a plastic stirring rod, to sequentially dip into the colored liquids. They first dip the tool into the light blue liquid, then the red, then the dark blue/black, stirring each time. Finally, the tool, now visibly stained dark blue from the previous dip, is immersed into the beaker with the clear liquid, which immediately begins to turn blue as the residue washes off the tool. This action follows the audio instruction to proceed from "lightest to darkest" in terms of the initial colored solutions.

A person wearing a light blue lab coat and purple gloves is shown performing a lab procedure. Initially, they are using a thin, rod-like instrument to stir a blue substance in one of four small, cylindrical glass containers, which hold different colored liquids: red, black, blue, and a lighter blue/green. The containers are arranged on a white surface, likely a lab bench covered with a paper mat. After stirring, the person removes the rod, and the camera then cuts to a closer view of their gloved hands. They are holding a rectangular glass slide that has a purple smear on it, and they are carefully wiping the back of the slide with a small piece of white, cotton-like material. Faint text, possibly "1.A" or "TA", is visible on the top edge of the slide.

The video opens with a gloved hand, wearing a blue surgical glove, carefully placing a transparent glass microscope slide onto a white, textured laboratory surface. The slide has a purple-colored liquid sample on it and a handwritten label that appears to read "D.J. Smith" followed by numbers. The camera then pans right to reveal a row of six similar glass slides laid out on the white surface. Each slide contains a blood smear, which varies in appearance and color intensity, from light pink to dark purple. All slides have a white label with black numbers, such as "D09 C 01142", "15 C 28451", "D07 F 33943", "D09 C 24927", "D08 F 21331", and "15 C 38426". As the camera continues to show the slides, text overlays appear at the bottom of the screen, stating "Examples of 5 Poor Smears and One Good Blood Smear". Each slide is then individually labeled below it: the first slide on the left is marked "2 smears on one", the second "Too thick", the third "Squash prep", the fourth "Too thin", the fifth "Flies!", and the sixth (far right) "Good smear". The video then fades to black.
